name: A* Search
tag: Ranks paths by known cost plus an estimate of remaining cost
history: A* expands the frontier state with the smallest f(n)=g(n)+h(n). An admissible heuristic does not overestimate remaining cost; consistency additionally keeps estimated costs monotone along edges.
why: It can find optimal paths while exploring far fewer states than uninformed shortest-path search.
problemItSolves: It focuses expensive route search toward a goal by using domain knowledge as a heuristic.

name: Agent2Agent (A2A) Protocol
tag: Agent to agent communication for discovery, delegation, and task results
history: A2A defines a common way for agents from different systems to communicate without exposing their internal implementation. Agent Cards describe capabilities and connection requirements, while messages and tasks carry interactions and work results. It complements MCP's tool and context interfaces with an agent-to-agent communication layer.
why: Useful when independently built agents need to delegate work, track progress, and exchange outputs. Protocol compatibility does not establish that a remote agent is trustworthy.

name: Agent Harness
tag: Wraps a model with instructions, tools, state, policies, and an execution loop
history: An agent harness is the application layer around a model that assembles context, exposes capabilities, executes actions, records results, and decides when a run pauses or ends. The model proposes behavior; the harness owns the operational boundary.
why: It turns a stateless model call into a controllable, observable system that can complete multi-step work.

why: Bun reduces backend tool sprawl by combining runtime, package manager, test runner, and bundling utilities in one fast tool. This can cut install time, simplify scripts, and improve local dev speed compared with stitching many separate tools together.
challenges: Create a new Bun project, add a start script, and run it with bun run. Capture startup time and compare to Node on your device.

name: Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
tag: Building subword tokens by repeatedly merging frequent adjacent units
history: BPE originated as a compression method and was adapted for open-vocabulary neural machine translation. Starting from small units, training repeatedly merges frequent adjacent pairs into vocabulary entries.
why: BPE balances a manageable vocabulary with shorter sequences for frequent patterns. The learned merges are corpus-dependent and do not necessarily align with words or meaningful morphemes.
challenges: Describe the merge rule: During standard BPE vocabulary learning, what is repeatedly added?
Handle rare words: How can BPE represent a rare word absent as a complete vocabulary entry?
Recognize corpus dependence: Why can two BPE tokenizers split the same word differently?
Evaluate vocabulary tradeoffs: What is a typical effect of a much larger BPE vocabulary?
Avoid semantic assumptions: Which conclusion about a BPE token boundary is unsafe?

extension.problemItSolves: BPE balances a manageable vocabulary with shorter sequences for frequent patterns. The learned merges are corpus-dependent and do not necessarily align with words or meaningful morphemes.

name: Apache Cassandra
tag: a distributed wide-column nosql database
history: Created at Facebook by Avinash Lakshman and Prashant Malik (2008). Open-sourced by Facebook in 2008. Entered the Apache Incubator in 2009. Became an Apache Top-Level Project in 2010. Influenced by Amazon Dynamo (distribution) and Google Bigtable (data model).
why: Cassandra solves always-on, high-write, globally distributed data storage where horizontal scale, fault tolerance, and tunable consistency matter more than complex joins or strict single-node ACID behavior.
challenges: Design a table for 'latest orders by user'. Pick partition key and clustering columns, then explain how your design avoids cross-partition scans.

name: Cloudflare
tag: edge network for security, speed, and serverless
history: Founded in 2009 by Matthew Prince, Michelle Zatlyn, and Lee Holloway. Early growth came from reverse-proxy CDN performance plus DDoS mitigation and security. Became widely adopted for DNS and edge protection in front of web applications. Introduced Cloudflare Workers to run JavaScript/Web API-style serverless code at the edge. Expanded from web acceleration into developer platform, storage, and Zero Trust enterprise networking.
why: Cloudflare reduces latency, improves uptime, and blocks attacks by placing security and application logic at a globally distributed edge network. Teams use it to combine CDN, DNS, DDoS protection, WAF, Zero Trust access, and edge/serverless compute in one platform.

name: CNN (Convolutional Neural Network)
tag: neural networks that learn local spatial features
history: LeNet demonstrated convolutional networks for handwritten character recognition in the 1990s. AlexNet's 2012 ImageNet result helped popularize deeper CNNs. Later architectures explored greater depth, multi-scale processing, and residual connections. CNN describes a family of architectures, not a single product or release.
why: CNNs reuse learned filters across local regions, producing feature maps that can capture increasingly complex patterns. This structure is useful for image classification and other vision tasks. The Data category groups this concept with its implementation tools: PyTorch and TensorFlow, often used through Python. None of these specific tools is required by the mathematical architecture.
challenges: Apply a 3x3 filter to a small grid by hand and explain weight sharing.
Calculate the output dimensions of a convolution with specified stride and padding.
Build a small image classifier and inspect every layer's output shape.
Compare training and validation curves and diagnose overfitting.
Evaluate a pretrained CNN on held-out images and report per-class errors.

extension.problemItSolves: Learns features from spatially structured inputs instead of relying entirely on manually designed image descriptors. Local connectivity and shared weights reduce parameters relative to a fully connected layer on the same input. Pooling or strided convolutions can reduce spatial resolution; pooling is not mandatory.
latestChanges: Reference snapshot: September 9, 2026. CNN is an architecture family with no single latest version.
TensorFlow's introductory tutorial trains a convolutional image classifier; PyTorch's tutorial demonstrates a LeNet-style network and automatic differentiation.

name: HashiCorp Consul
tag: service discovery and networking control plane

Connect introduced service mesh capabilities, including mTLS and intentions. Consul expanded with Kubernetes integrations and multi-cluster networking patterns like peering.
why: Consul helps distributed systems find each other, stay health-aware, and enforce service-to-service security policies across VMs, containers, and multiple environments.

history: 2016: dbt was open-sourced by Fishtown Analytics. 2019: Fishtown Analytics rebranded to dbt Labs. Early 2020s: dbt helped define the analytics engineering role. Later releases added semantic-layer and mesh-oriented governance patterns.
why: dbt turns raw warehouse tables into trusted analytics models using version-controlled SQL. It adds testing, documentation, lineage, and deployment patterns so data teams can ship reliable transformations faster.

name: DPO (Direct Preference Optimization)
tag: Direct preference optimization using chosen and rejected response pairs
history: Direct Preference Optimization was introduced as a way to train language models directly from preference pairs. Its standard objective compares the policy's relative likelihoods of preferred and rejected responses with those of a reference policy. This avoids fitting a separate explicit reward model and running an online reinforcement-learning loop during standard DPO training.
why: Simplifies preference-based adaptation when a dataset of response comparisons is available. Preference quality, reference choice, and evaluation still matter; a lower training loss alone does not establish a better assistant.
challenges: Create a preference example with one prompt, a chosen response, and a rejected response.

name: GitHub Actions

why: GitHub Actions automates build, test, release, and deployment steps directly from repository events, reducing manual DevOps work and improving delivery speed, consistency, and auditability.
challenges: Create .github/workflows/ci.yml to run npm ci and npm test on push and pull_request to main.

Extract shared test logic into a reusable workflow and call it from two repositories.
Harden a workflow with least-privilege permissions, pinned action SHAs, and dependency review checks.

codeDropdown.instructions: Complete the workflow so it runs Node.js tests on both push and pull requests to main using a matrix.
codeDropdown.template:
name: node-ci
on:
  {{blank1}}:
    branches: [main]
  {{blank2}}:
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: {{blank3}}
    strategy:
      matrix:
        node: [18, 20]
    steps:
      - uses: {{blank4}}
      - uses: {{blank5}}
        with:
          node-version: ${{ matrix.node }}
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm test

mobileUxNotes: Prioritize large touch targets and short prompts.
Prefer dropdown code blanks over free-form typing on mobile.
Keep each assessment step under ~60 seconds.

name: GitLab CI/CD
tag: integrated pipelines for build, test, and deploy
history: GitLab CI started as a separate project before being integrated into core GitLab around the GitLab 8.x era. name: MariaDB
tag: open-source relational database server
history: 2009: MariaDB was started by Michael "Monty" Widenius as a MySQL fork. It emerged after concern about MySQL stewardship following Oracle's Sun acquisition. MariaDB kept strong MySQL protocol and SQL compatibility to reduce migration friction. Over time it added MariaDB-specific capabilities and diverged in some features/behavior. The MariaDB Foundation supports community development, with commercial support also available.
why: MariaDB provides a reliable SQL database for transactional apps, analytics-friendly querying, and MySQL-oriented migration paths while staying open source and self-hostable.

name: OODA Loop for Agents

name: OpenID Connect
tag: identity layer for oauth 2.0 authentication
history: Created by the OpenID Foundation as the modern successor to OpenID 2.0. OpenID Connect Core 1.0 was finalized in 2014. It became the default web/mobile SSO choice for consumer and enterprise identity. Now considered mature/legacy in many stacks, but still heavily deployed and operationally critical.
why: OpenID Connect standardizes user authentication on top of OAuth 2.0, so apps can verify who a user is (ID token), fetch basic profile claims, and avoid building custom login protocols per provider.
challenges: Given a decoded ID token payload, identify issuer (iss), audience (aud), subject (sub), expiration (exp), and nonce. State whether the token should be accepted.

You inherit an SPA using implicit flow. List concrete migration steps to Code + PKCE and explain how this changes token exposure risk.
A login fails with 'invalid_audience'. Check discovery metadata, client_id usage, and ID token aud/azp logic. Propose a minimal fix plan.
Choose the smallest scope set to satisfy: sign-in, display name, and email verification status. Explain tradeoffs in privacy and UX.

name: OpenTelemetry (opentelemetry)
tag: open standard for app telemetry collection
history: 2019: OpenTracing and OpenCensus merged under CNCF to form OpenTelemetry. Tracing became the earliest stable signal and drove broad early adoption. Metrics support later stabilized across core APIs/SDKs, enabling full-stack observability workflows. The OpenTelemetry Collector became a central deployment pattern for routing and processing telemetry.
why: OpenTelemetry standardizes how apps emit traces, metrics, and logs so teams avoid vendor lock-in and duplicated instrumentation work. It gives a common pipeline (SDKs + Collector + OTLP) to observe distributed systems consistently.
challenges: Auto-instrument a small HTTP service and confirm one request trace appears via a local debug exporter.
Send OTLP traces from your app to an OpenTelemetry Collector, add batch processing, and export to your tracing backend.
Add trace_id to logs, create a latency metric dashboard, and document how you jump from alert -> metric -> trace -> logs.
Implement head-based sampling and compare error investigations before vs after sampling changes.
Add memory limiter + retry/queue settings in Collector and validate behavior under load spikes.

extension.tag: open standard for app telemetry collection
latestChanges: Collector and SDK releases continue frequently with performance and stability improvements.
OTLP over gRPC/HTTP remains the default vendor-neutral export path.
Semantic conventions are versioned more explicitly, making upgrades safer.

name: RabbitMQ
tag: message broker for reliable async communication
history: RabbitMQ began in 2007 as an open-source AMQP message broker. It is implemented in Erlang/OTP, leveraging the BEAM runtime for concurrency and fault tolerance. RabbitMQ 3.8 introduced quorum queues (Raft-based replication) for stronger data safety. RabbitMQ 3.9 introduced streams for high-throughput, log-style messaging workloads. RabbitMQ 4.x removes classic mirrored queues and reinforces modern queue/stream patterns.
why: RabbitMQ decouples backend services with asynchronous messaging so systems can handle traffic spikes, isolate failures, retry work, and route events reliably.
challenges: Create a producer/consumer pair where tasks survive broker restarts and are manually acknowledged.
Implement a retry queue with TTL and dead-letter exchange to reprocess failed jobs up to 3 times.

Plan a migration from classic mirrored queues to quorum queues with minimal downtime and rollback steps.
Add metrics and alerts for queue depth, consumer lag, unacked messages, and connection churn; define SLOs.

name: Reranking
tag: Rescoring retrieved candidates with a more precise relevance model
history: Two-stage retrieval first gathers candidates quickly, then applies a costlier reranker to a smaller set. Cross-encoders can jointly inspect query and document tokens for more precise relevance scoring.

name: REST
tag: architectural style for stateless web apis
history: REST was defined by Roy Fielding in his 2000 dissertation as an architectural style, not a protocol. It emerged from lessons learned while designing the early web architecture. Core constraints include client-server, statelessness, cacheability, uniform interface, layered system, and optional code-on-demand. REST became the dominant public API style in the 2010s and remains foundational, though now considered mature/legacy in many stacks.
why: REST provides a consistent way to expose and consume resources over the web so clients and servers can evolve independently, scale horizontally, and use standard HTTP features like caching and status codes.
challenges: Given a Todo resource, choose GET/POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE routes and matching success status codes (200, 201, 204). Keep routes noun-based.
Design GET /products with pagination, filtering, ETag, and 304 handling. Include sample request/response headers.

Propose a v1 to v2 migration plan using additive changes, deprecation headers, and compatibility tests.
Define a reusable error response schema (code, message, details, traceId) and map it to 400/401/403/404/409/422/500.

extension.tag: architectural style for stateless web apis
latestChanges: HTTP semantics were consolidated in RFC 9110 (2022), clarifying method and status code behavior used by REST APIs.
HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 improved transport speed and multiplexing, while REST constraints remained unchanged.
Modern REST practice now commonly includes OpenAPI contracts, linting, and contract testing for consistency.
extension.problemItSolves: REST provides a consistent way to expose and consume resources over the web so clients and servers can evolve independently, scale horizontally, and use standard HTTP features like caching and status codes.

history: RLAIF uses AI-generated judgments to supply feedback for reinforcement learning. Constitutional AI demonstrated a pipeline in which model comparisons train a preference model, whose rewards guide policy updates. Later work also studied obtaining rewards directly from an AI evaluator.
why: Useful when human preference labeling is difficult to scale. Evaluator quality and the chosen criteria still need independent human checks.

name: RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback)
tag: Learning desired behavior from human preference feedback
history: RLHF uses human judgments to shape a learning system's reward signal. Work on learning from comparisons of behavior helped establish the approach before it was applied to instruction-following language models. A common pipeline learns a reward model from preferences and optimizes a policy against it; PPO is one possible optimizer, not the definition of RLHF.
why: Helps train for qualities people can compare more easily than they can specify as exact rules. Its results depend on whose preferences are collected and whether the learned reward reflects the intended behavior.
challenges: Write a rubric for comparing two assistant responses on helpfulness and accuracy.
Label ten response pairs and record disagreements between reviewers.
Sketch the separate roles of the policy, reward model, and reference policy.
Construct a response that could exploit a reward model's preference for length.
Design a held-out human evaluation that is independent of the training reward.

extension.problemItSolves: Converts human judgments into a training signal for behavior that is difficult to express with a hand-written reward function.

name: TLS (Transport Layer Security)
tag: protocol that encrypts data in transit
history: SSL 2.0/3.0 had serious weaknesses; TLS 1.0 replaced SSL 3.0 in 1999. TLS 1.2 (2008) improved algorithm agility and enabled stronger cipher choices. High-profile attacks (BEAST, POODLE, Heartbleed impact on implementations) pushed stricter configs. TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446, 2018) removed many legacy features and reduced handshake latency. Legacy versions/ciphers remain a migration concern in old enterprise systems.
why: TLS protects data over networks from eavesdropping, tampering, and impersonation by providing encryption, integrity checks, and endpoint authentication.
challenges: Given a config that allows TLS 1.0 and RSA key exchange, list two concrete risks and one immediate fix.

name: Vision Transformer (ViT)
tag: image patches processed with transformer attention
history: Dosovitskiy and colleagues introduced ViT in an October 2020 preprint, subsequently published at ICLR 2021. The work applied a Transformer to sequences of image patches and demonstrated strong image-recognition results after large-scale pretraining. ViT is an architecture family, not a product with one current release.
why: ViT embeds image patches as tokens, adds positional information, and processes them with Transformer blocks. Self-attention relates patches across the image. CNNs provide a useful comparison because their local filters encode different architectural assumptions. Neither approach is universally superior: compare accuracy, pretraining data, compute, and latency on the same task.
challenges: Split a 224x224 image into non-overlapping 16x16 patches and count the tokens.

extension.problemItSolves: Provides an attention-based way to learn image representations. Standard global self-attention models relationships between all patch tokens; its pairwise attention computation grows quadratically with sequence length. Smaller patches or larger images increase the token count.

name: WebRTC
tag: browser api for real-time media and data
history: 2010–2011: Technology from GIPS was open-sourced by Google and evolved into WebRTC. Standardization split: W3C defined browser APIs, while IETF defined transport/signaling-related protocols (ICE, STUN/TURN usage, RTP/DTLS/SRTP, SDP/JSEP flow). WebRTC replaced plugin-era real-time web communication approaches (for example Flash-based calling stacks). By the late 2010s, cross-browser support became practical; today it is a mature, foundational real-time web stack often treated as a 'legacy baseline' in product architecture.
why: WebRTC enables low-latency peer-to-peer audio, video, and arbitrary data exchange in browsers/apps without requiring plugins, while still supporting relay fallback when direct peer paths fail.
challenges: Draw the exact signaling sequence for a browser-to-browser data chat: offer, answer, ICE candidate exchange, and connected state checks.
